title: Min Stack
prompt:
Design a stack that supports `push(val)`, `pop()`, `top()`, and `getMin()`, where `getMin()` retrieves the minimum element in the stack, all in O(1) time.

You'll implement this as a single function `run_min_stack_ops(ops)`, where `ops` is an array of `[operationName, argument]` pairs (argument is `null` for `pop`, `top`, and `getMin`), applied in order to one stack instance. `push` never produces output; `pop`, `top`, and `getMin` each push their result onto the output array, in call order. Return the output array. It is guaranteed `pop`, `top`, and `getMin` are never called on an empty stack.

examples.explanation: After pushing -2, 0, -3, the min is -3. Popping removes -3, top is now 0, and the min is back to -2.
Pushing the same value twice still tracks the minimum correctly even after one copy is popped, since the min-stack keeps one entry per push.
With a single element on the stack, both top() and getMin() trivially return that same value.

constraints: pop, top, and getMin operations are always called on a non-empty stack
hints: Tracking the minimum by rescanning the stack on every getMin() costs O(n) per call — you need O(1).
Keep a second stack that tracks the running minimum alongside the main stack.

Push the current minimum (min of the new value and the previous running minimum) onto the min-stack every time you push to the main stack, so both stacks always stay the same size and popping either is trivial.

solution.approach: Maintain two stacks in parallel: the main stack holding actual values, and a min-stack where each position holds the minimum of all elements up to that point in the main stack. On push, push the value to the main stack and push min(value, current min-stack top) to the min-stack. On pop, pop both stacks together. getMin() is just the min-stack's top, and top() is the main stack's top — all O(1) since both stacks move in lockstep.
